---
The precision-recall plots further distinguished method performance across conditions (**Fig 3C**). IBD occupied a consistently favorable region of precision-recall space, high recall combined with relatively high precision across baseline, recombination sweep, and migration conditions. IBS and Phylo showed greater displacement toward lower precision or lower recall depending on the condition, with migration appearing to reduce precision most markedly for IBS. The overall ranking of methods reveals a consistent pattern alongside one notable feature, placed IBD as the top-ranked method (rank 1) across all three scenarios. Under the baseline scenario, IBS ranks second and phylogenetic distances third at the operating point used to construct the ranking. However, this ordering differs, with phylogenetic ranking second and IBS third under the recombination sweep and migration scenarios (**Fig 3D**), with a pattern that may reflect differential sensitivity of these metrics to segment-level fragmentation versus topological signal at the specific threshold examined.

To evaluate how robust each method remains under demographic perturbations, we quantified the mean AUPRC across a range of bottleneck population sizes. This analysis was conducted under two recombination regimes, moderate ($10^{-7}$) and extremely low ($10^{-9}$), and limited to transmission events occurring within 25 generations. Mean AUPRC for all methods differed markedly between the two recombination rate conditions tested (**Supplementary Figure S2**). At the medium recombination rate, all three methods exceeded or approached the 0.60 reference threshold (dashed line) across both bottleneck sizes. IBD achieved the highest mean AUPRC (\~0.67) under Ne bottleneck = 5×1000, with IBS (\~0.62) and Phylo (\~0.60) closely following. Under Ne bottleneck = 20×1000 at the same recombination rate, AUPRC values for all three methods were marginally lower but remained clustered in a narrow range (\~0.59–0.66), with confidence intervals that did not overlap substantially between IBD and Phylo. Across both bottleneck sizes at the medium recombination rate, the ordering of methods was consistent, IBD \> IBS \> Phylo, and inter-method differences were modest.

At the very low recombination rate, the pattern diverged substantially from the medium recombination condition. Under Ne bottleneck = 1×1000, all three methods fell below the 0.60 reference threshold, with IBD recording a mean AUPRC of approximately 0.49, IBS approximately 0.33, and Phylo approximately 0.26. The magnitude of the inter-method gap widened considerably compared to the medium recombination condition, and all confidence intervals remained narrow, indicating that the reduced performance was consistent across replicates rather than driven by variability. Notably, only a single bottleneck size was represented in the very low recombination panel, precluding direct comparison of bottleneck size effects within that condition. Taken together, recombination rate emerged as a stronger modulator of absolute AUPRC than bottleneck population size, with the transition from medium to very low recombination associated with a decline of approximately 0.18–0.34 AUPRC units depending on method.

\vspace{5mm}

![](../results/main/figure3_method_performance.pdf)

***Figure 3:** Comparative recoverability of true transmission links across genomic inference layers and biological scenarios. Top left: distributions of sensitivity (TP / (TP + FN)) for IBD, IBS, and phylogenetic inference across four scenarios (baseline, recombination sweep, migration; distinguished by color). Top right: corresponding false discovery rate (FP / (TP + FP)) distributions for the same methods and scenarios. Middle: precision–recall curves for IBD, IBS, and phylogenetic patristic distances across three scenarios (baseline, recombination sweep, migration), shown as separate facets with recall on the x-axis (0–1) and precision on the y-axis (0–1). Bottom: ranked performance table showing the ordinal rank of each method (1 = best) within each scenario across three evaluation criteria, with ranks displayed for IBD, IBS, and phylogenetic patristic distances under baseline, recombination sweep, and migration conditions.*
---

At a fixed 90% specificity operating point, sensitivity displayed a pattern diverging from the AUPRC gradient: all three methods showed the highest sensitivity at the lowest recombination rate ($10^{-9}$), declining sharply at $10^{-8}$ before partially recovering at higher rates, and migration rate had negligible effect on these trajectories (**Fig 6E-H, Supplementary Fig S3**). IBD exhibited the steepest initial decline, from approximately 0.63–0.67 at $10^{-9}$ to approximately 0.34–0.40 at $10^{-9}$, with values stabilizing between 0.35 and 0.45 across the two highest recombination rates; IBS and Phylo followed similar trajectories but from lower starting values (\~0.46–0.51 and \~0.29–0.30, respectively), with Phylo showing near-flat sensitivity across recombination rates above $10^{-9}$. Complementing this, the fraction of replicates classified as identifiable was essentially confined to the $10^{-9}$ condition (**Supplementary Fig S4**): IBD achieved identifiable status in 95%, 70%, and 73% of replicates at migration rates of 0.001, 0.01, and 0.05 respectively, while IBS achieved identifiability in only 3–15% of replicates under the same condition, and Phylo returned 0.00 across all recombination and migration combinations. At recombination rates of $10^{-9}$ and above, the identifiable fraction dropped to 0.00 for all methods regardless of migration rate, indicating a hard identifiability boundary determined by recombination rather than population structure.

The IBD advantage over the next-best method, quantified as the AUPRC gap across the full recombination-by-migration grid, was largest at $10^{-9}$ (0.158–0.176 across migration rates), narrowed substantially at intermediate recombination rates (0.049–0.081 at $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-7}$), and partially widened again at $10^{-6}$ (0.085–0.095), with migration rate exerting minimal influence on gap magnitude within any recombination rate stratum (**Supplementary Fig S5**). Stratification by generational depth (G threshold) further revealed that AUPRC improved with increasing G for all methods and recombination rates, but the gain was differentially distributed: IBD maintained comparatively stable AUPRC across G thresholds at low recombination (0.42–0.49 at $10^{-9}$ from G=1 to G=25), whereas IBS and Phylo showed pronounced AUPRC deterioration at low recombination as G decreased, reaching values as low as 0.32 and 0.25 respectively at G=25 and $10^{-9}$ (**Supplementary Fig S7, Supplementary Table S3**). At higher recombination rates, the three methods converged toward comparable AUPRC values at G=25, with IBD, IBS, and Phylo reaching 0.71, 0.62, and 0.60 at $10^{-6}$, respectively, indicating that the relative advantage of IBD over competing methods was most pronounced under the joint condition of low recombination and broad generational windows.



The IBD advantage over the next-best method (**Fig. 7D**) remained structurally identical to that reported in supplementary analyses: the gap was largest at $10^{-9}$ (0.158–0.176 across migration rates) and narrowest at $10^{-7}$ (0.049–0.050), with a partial widening at $10^{-6}$ (0.085–0.095), and migration rate had no systematic directional effect on gap magnitude within any recombination stratum. The continuous identifiability phase diagram (**Supplementary Fig S8**) reinforced these patterns by mapping best AUPRC as a smooth surface across the full sample size range (100–400) at each migration rate. The dominant gradient in all three panels ran along the recombination axis, with the transition from low (red, ~0.5) to high (green, ~0.8+) AUPRC occurring sharply between approximately $10^{-8}$ and $10^{-6}$. The AUPRC = 0.80 threshold contour (dashed line) was reached only in restricted regions of the parameter space — specifically at small sample sizes combined with the highest recombination rates — and was absent entirely under migration = 0.01 within the tested range. Under migration = 0.001, the 0.80 contour was confined to recombination rates near $10^{-6}$ and sample sizes below approximately 175, while under migration = 0.05 the same contour extended to slightly lower recombination rates at the smallest sample sizes, indicating that the boundary of high recoverability is sensitive to the joint interaction of all three parameters but remains primarily gated by recombination rate.
